theme: Job’s integrity; the hymn to wisdom, where shall it be found?
readingInstruction: Read Job 27:1-28:28. Job holds to his integrity in chapter 27, and in chapter 28 there is a famous poem about wisdom. Notice how the poem is built: first a long description of what human beings can find, then a question about what they cannot.
settingTheScene: Zophar has not replied, and the three friends fall silent. Job speaks on, and in the next three chapters he gives his final defense. Chapter 27 is a vow to keep his integrity. Chapter 28 is different in tone and in kind. It is a hymn on wisdom that sounds almost like Proverbs, and some scholars think it is the narrator’s own voice. Whatever its source, it is placed at the center of the book, and it gives the book’s central answer to the question of how a person can find wisdom in a world of suffering.
observation: Job swears an oath: “As God lives, who has taken away my right, and the Almighty, who has made my soul bitter” (27:2).
He says that as long as he has breath, “my lips will not speak falsehood” (27:3-4).
“Far be it from me to say that you are right; till I die I will not put away my integrity from me” (27:5).
“I hold fast my righteousness and will not let it go; my heart does not reproach me for any of my days” (27:6).
Chapter 28 begins with mining: “Surely there is a mine for silver, and a place where gold is refined” (28:1).
Humans dig “a shaft in a valley away from where anyone lives” and “overturn mountains by the roots” (28:4, 9).
“But where shall wisdom be found? And where is the place of understanding?” (28:12).
It cannot be bought for gold or silver or onyx or sapphire (28:15-19).
“God understands the way to it, and he knows its place” (28:23).
“Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding” (28:28).
interpretation:
Chapter 27 is Job’s refusal to be pushed into a false confession. The friends have told him many times to repent, and he cannot, because he knows that he has not done what they say. He is not claiming to be sinless. He is saying that he did not bring this suffering on himself. To say otherwise would be to lie, and he will not lie even to please God, because he believes that God does not want his lies. This is a quiet kind of courage.

Then chapter 28 shifts the whole mood. The poem begins by describing the astonishing ability of human beings. We dig deep into the earth, we find silver and gold and sapphires, we reach places where birds and lions have never been. There is nothing human beings cannot find with enough labor. This is the picture of a technological, adventurous people.

And then the poem asks the question that all of that effort cannot answer: “But where shall wisdom be found?” It is hidden even from the eagle and the vulture. You cannot buy it. You cannot mine it. Death and the Abyss say, “We have heard a rumor of it.” The whole point of the poem is that wisdom is not something people can find by digging. It is not an object. It belongs to God.

The answer, which comes in verse 23, is that God knows its place, because God made the world by it. And then verse 28 states what he has told humankind: “The fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding.” This is the same line that opens the book of Proverbs (1:7). It is where wisdom begins and also where it ends.

Placed here, in the middle of Job’s suffering, the verse is a challenge and a comfort. Job does not have answers about why he is suffering. But he is being told that wisdom is not the same as having answers. It is fearing God, and refusing evil, in the dark.
connection: Proverbs 1:7 and 9:10 open and close their wisdom with the same line as verse 28. In the New Testament, Christ is “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), and in him “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). James 1:5 invites us: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all.”
application:
When you are tempted to say what is easy rather than what is true, remember Job. Your integrity is worth protecting. Ask God for the courage to say true things even when it costs you.

Think about where you go for wisdom. Is it a podcast, a person, a book? Ask whether you are first going to God and his word.

Pray that the “fear of the Lord” becomes your first instinct, and not just a phrase.
prayerPrompts: Tell God where you need wisdom you cannot find on your own.
Ask him for a heart that fears him and turns from evil.
Thank Jesus, in whom all wisdom is found.
